Trucebreakers
trūs'brāk-ərz
n. pl. (covenant-breakers; men who will not be bound by an agreement they have made)
English truce, from Middle English trewes, pledges of faith, with breaker. The Greek aspondos means literally without a drink-offering — without the libation that sealed a treaty, and so a man with whom no terms can be made.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, in the catalogue of the perilous times: “Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” (2Ti 3:3). Its neighbours in the list show the register. These are not petty offences but the dissolution of the bonds that hold a society upright: affection that no longer holds within a family, agreements that no longer hold between men, appetite that no longer holds within a man. Paul has already said what kind of season this is: “This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come” (2Ti 3:1). Romans uses the near-identical charge of the heathen mind: “Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” (Rom 1:31). Against this Scripture sets the man God receives, described by an oath he keeps at his own cost: “He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psa 15:4). Joshua's princes are the great narrative example. Deceived into a league with the Gibeonites, they still said, “We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them” (Jos 9:19) — and four hundred years later God avenged Saul's breach of that same word.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a trucebreaker as one who violates a truce, covenant or engagement; a truce being a suspension of arms by agreement, and, more broadly, a pledge of faith between parties.

expand to see more

TRUCE, n. [from trew, trewes, faith, pledge of faith.] A suspension of arms by agreement of the commanders; a temporary cessation of hostilities.

2. Intermission of action, pain or contest; temporary cessation.

TRUCEBREAKER, n. One who violates a truce, covenant or engagement.

Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers. 2 Tim. iii.

Key Scripture

2Ti 3:3 — "Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,"

2Ti 3:1 — "This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come."

Psa 15:4 — "In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."

Jos 9:19 — "But all the princes said unto all the congregation, We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them."

Modern Corruption

An oath is now held to bind only while it still suits the one who swore it, which is precisely the definition of a trucebreaker.

expand to see more

The plainest place this shows is the marriage covenant, where vows are made in the language of permanence and dissolved on the ground that the parties have changed. The reasoning is always the same and it is always the reasoning of 2 Timothy 3:3: the agreement was made by a man who no longer exists, therefore it no longer binds. Scripture's answer is Psalm 15:4, which describes the citizen of God's hill by exactly the case that tests him — he swore, the swearing turned out to cost him, and he did not change. The verse assumes the hurt. An oath that costs nothing has not yet been kept. The same collapse works its way through commercial dealing, church membership, and the ordinary promises of a household, and in each case the word given is treated as a forecast of intention rather than a bond upon the will.

The Greek word carries a detail worth keeping. Aspondos is without a libation — treaties in the ancient world were sealed with a poured drink offering, so a man called aspondos is one with whom no terms can be struck at all: not merely a man who breaks a truce, but a man no truce can hold. That is the terminal stage, and it is why the word sits beside implacable in Romans 1:31. The remedy is not sterner contracts. It is a nature that keeps faith because it has been dealt with faithfully — and here the doctrine of the covenant is the whole comfort of the Christian, because the covenant of grace does not rest on the sinner's constancy but on the oath of God, who sware by himself since he could swear by no greater. A people who know they are held by an unbreakable word are the only people likely to keep their own.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aspondos (G786), without a libation, admitting no truce; asunthetos (G802), covenant-breaking; Hebrew shaba (H7650), to swear an oath.

expand to see more

Greek aspondos (G786) — without a drink offering, hence admitting of no truce or agreement; rendered trucebreakers; 2 Timothy 3:3.

Greek asunthetos (G802) — not put together, covenant-breaking; the parallel charge in the heathen catalogue; Romans 1:31.

Hebrew shaba (H7650) — to swear, to bind oneself by seven, that is by an oath; Joshua 9:19, Psalm 15:4.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant, a bond cut and sealed; the whole framework the trucebreaker despises; Genesis 15:18.

Greek horkos (G3727) — an oath; God interposed himself by an oath to show the immutability of his counsel; Hebrews 6:17.

Usage

"“Trucebreakers, false accusers” — the bonds of a society coming apart in one list."

"“He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” — the oath that costs, kept."

"“We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel” — a word kept though it was got by deceit."
